projects.title: Coffee Chain Store Performance Analysis
projects.tagline: Why do some of a coffee chain's 12 shops earn four times more than others? Descriptive statistics, correlation, regression and probability, across Excel, Python and R.

dataset.name: The Corner Cup store data (course case-study dataset)
dataset.note: A fictional chain of 12 coffee shops supplied for the course: location type, floor size, staff, daily customers, average spend per customer, monthly revenue and customer satisfaction. 12 rows and 8 columns, with no missing values.

projects.cover_alt: Scatter plot of the 12 shops with a rising regression line

request.label: Request the project files
request.intro: The Excel workbook, Python notebook, R script and full written report are available on request.
request.message: Hi Fathima, I'd like to see more of your coffee chain store performance analysis (the Excel workbook, Python notebook and R script). Could you share them?

projects.business_problem: The owner of The Corner Cup runs 12 coffee shops, 7 in the city and 5 in the suburbs, and has big decisions ahead: which shops to grow, which need help, and where to open next. Revenue ranges from $32.3K to $131K a month. The question was what actually drives that gap, and what she should do about it.

highlights.label: Daily customers and revenue
highlights.note: The strongest link in the data

highlights.label: Of revenue differences explained
highlights.note: Regression on daily customers, R² = 0.77, p < 0.001

highlights.label: Monthly revenue per extra daily customer

approach: Excel: frequency table, summary statistics and coefficient of variation, then an urban vs suburban comparison with a two-sample t-test.
Python: loaded and checked the data with pandas, built a histogram, scatter plot and box plot, and a correlation matrix with a heat map.
R: fitted a simple linear regression of revenue on daily customers, predicted revenue for a new 300-customer shop, and answered planning questions with the binomial and Poisson distributions.
Turned the results into three recommendations for the owner, each with its evidence and a concrete action.
projects.visuals_intro: Hover over any chart to see each shop's numbers, or switch to the table view. All values are calculated from the 12-shop dataset.

charts.title: Daily customers vs monthly revenue
charts.caption: Busier shops earn more: each point is a shop and the dashed line is the regression fit. Airport Terminal (441 customers a day) sits about $27.5K below the line because its customers spend the least, while suburban Tech Campus earns more than most city shops.

charts.title: Monthly revenue by shop
charts.caption: Revenue ranges from $32.3K to $131K, about four times apart. Only 4 of the 12 shops earn more than $80K a month.

charts.title: What moves with revenue? (correlation, r)
charts.caption: Foot traffic stands out. The other four factors move together (bigger, better-staffed shops with higher spend and happier customers) but bigger shops do not attract more customers. Correlation shows a link, not cause and effect.

comparison.title: Urban vs suburban shops (averages)
comparison.note: City shops earn more because they are busier, not because customers spend more or are happier. The revenue gap is not statistically significant (Welch t-test, p = 0.071), so location type alone does not decide success.

projects.tabs_title: How it was done, tool by tool

subprojects.title: Excel: describe the data
subprojects.description: Descriptive statistics in an Excel workbook, built with formulas so every number can be traced.
steps: COUNTIF frequency table and bar chart of urban and suburban shops (7 and 5)
AVERAGE, MEDIAN, STDEV.S, MIN and MAX, plus the coefficient of variation to compare spread across units
AVERAGEIF group averages and a two-tailed T.TEST for the urban vs suburban revenue gap

chart.title: How much each measure varies (coefficient of variation)

subprojects.key_insight: Revenue and daily customers vary a lot from shop to shop, while spend per customer and satisfaction stay fairly steady. That pointed to foot traffic as the main source of the revenue gap.

subprojects.title: Python: visualise and correlate
subprojects.description: Exploration and charts in a Python notebook with pandas and matplotlib.
steps: Loaded the CSV with pandas and checked it with head(), info() and describe(); results matched Excel
Histogram of revenue, scatter plot of customers vs revenue by location, and box plot of satisfaction
Correlation matrix with data.corr() and a heat map
subprojects.key_insight: Revenue is slightly right-skewed (skewness 0.63): most shops earn $32K to $98K and Harbour View stands alone at $131K. Daily customers correlate with revenue at r = 0.88, far more than any other factor.

subprojects.title: R: regression and probability
subprojects.description: Modelling and probability questions in an R script, run in RStudio.
steps: lm(Monthly_Revenue_000 ~ Daily_Customers): Revenue ($000) = −2.785 + 0.276 × Daily customers, R² = 0.768
Predicted a new 300-customer shop at about $80.0K a month (95% prediction interval $47.3K to $112.7K)
Binomial model for 5 new suburban shops (40% chance each of becoming high-revenue) and a Poisson model of Airport Terminal arrivals (18 an hour)

chart.title: Of 5 new shops, how many become high-revenue? (binomial, p = 0.4)

subprojects.key_insight: About 2 of 5 new suburban shops should do well, with a 92.2% chance that at least one does and a 7.8% chance that none do. At the airport, a rush of 25 or more customers an hour happens about 6.8% of the time, roughly 1.6 hours a day.

insights: Foot traffic drives revenue: daily customers explain about 77% of the differences between shops (R² = 0.77), and each extra customer a day adds about $276 a month.
City shops earn $83.3K a month against $54.9K in the suburbs, but mainly because they are busier. Spend and satisfaction are almost the same, and the gap is not statistically significant (p = 0.071).
Airport Terminal is the busiest shop (441 a day) but has the lowest spend ($6.90) and satisfaction (3.5), and earns about $27.5K less than the model predicts.
Only 4 of 12 shops earn more than $80K a month, so the chance that a shop is high-revenue is 1 in 3.
recommendations: Choose new sites by foot traffic, not by the urban or suburban label. Count pedestrian traffic before signing a lease and aim for about 300 customers a day, the level the model links to an $80K shop.
Raise spend per customer at the Airport Terminal with combo deals and quick add-ons ($1 more per customer is about $13,000 a month), and add staff for the 25-plus-customer peaks.
Open new suburban shops in stages: 2 or 3 high-traffic sites first, review after 6 to 12 months, then decide on the rest.
improvements: With only 12 shops at one point in time, every estimate has wide uncertainty. Monthly data over a year would show trends and seasonality.
A multiple regression with daily customers and spend per customer together would likely explain much of the remaining 23%.
An interactive Power BI dashboard would let the owner explore each shop herself.
